chapter_theme: The account of the city ends with its ball grounds, mansions, palace and unceasing music; then the king Saccandan is praised as terrible to foes, refuge to the frightened, generous, learned and godlike, and at the height of his fame the poet turns to the princess of Vidaiyam and describes her beauty from hair to hips.

cast.role: king of Emangadam at Rajamapuram, Civakan's father
daughter of the king of Vidaiyam, Saccandan's queen and Civakan's mother

150.reading: The poet describes the grounds of the city where the young play with balls that look like gems set in gold and pearls, as if the sky's stars had been inlaid in rows.

151.reading: The many ways the ball is played, caught, hidden in a garland, run along the hand, struck in rows, made to dance like a hooded snake, give a pleasure without limit.
151.nuance: The verse is a catalogue of play moves; its last line, that the pleasure has no limit, sets the tone of unbounded delight the city enjoys before its fall.

152.reading: Elsewhere the noise swells from elephants with three streams of must whose tusks, sharp as Death, have borne the heads of angry kings like balls, mixed with wind-swift horses and chariots.
152.nuance: The ball of the previous two verses returns grimly: the war elephants are said to strike enemy kings' heads as balls, so the city's play and its violence share one image.

153.reading: The city has mansions where people sleep amid the sound of instruments, mansions of red gold holding the treasure enemies paid, and mansions where women with jasmine hair keep their jewels, and places beyond these without number.
153.nuance: The tribute of enemies (தெவ்வர் தந்த நீள் நிதி) is counted among the city's wealth: its luxury rests on conquest.

154.reading: Between flowering kongu, vengai and golden-clustered konrai trees stand the halls where women's dance never ceases and the temple fit to be praised by women like victory itself.
154.nuance: Line 1 reads பூத் கோங்கும், which looks like a dropped letter (for பூத்த); the sense of flowering is clear. Whether கோயில் here is a shrine or the royal palace is not fixed by this verse; the next verse uses கோயில் for the king's palace.

155.reading: The prince's palace, with pillars of polished gems, long walls of red gold and a roof laid in white gold, looks as if Indra's own city had come down here with all its rights.

156.reading: The sounds of dance, of songs that clap and melt the heart, of the drum and of the sweet lute blend so that the city passes every day in a sound that never fades.

157.reading: The king is introduced: Saccandan of the red lotus eyes, fierce in wrath as a poisonous serpent's fire, like nectar to those who come to him in fear, and a wounding goddess to women.
157.nuance: Three faces of one king in three lines: terror to enemies, refuge to the frightened, affliction to women. The third, அணங்கு, is the word the love poems use for the woman whose beauty wounds; here the king is the afflictor, before the story reverses it.

158.reading: Saccandan drove out want with his generous hand and the massed chariots of strong foes with his spear; his fragrant chest is the home of subtle learning and the place where Lakshmi's eyes rest.

159.reading: His cool white umbrella hung with pearls shades the whole sea-girt world alike, so the earth, resting in the shade of his feet as in a father's, rejoices in love for him.
159.nuance: The umbrella's shade is equal (உலகு ஒப்ப): the praise is of impartial protection, the straight sceptre seen as shade rather than as stick.

claims.claim: a king whose rule shelters all alike stands to the world as a father, and the world rejoices in that care

160.reading: The king of the great land is likened to gods one by one: to Dharma in cool grace, to Varuna in giving, to Death in taking life, to Vaman in something rare, and to the five-arrowed son of Tiru in beauty.
160.nuance: The list ends with Kama (திருமகன் with five arrows): beauty of the god of desire is made part of the king's divinity, which the story will turn against him. வாமனே in line 2 is hard to place: it may be Vishnu's dwarf form or a Jain name of the Arhat, and which quality it goes with (அருமையால், rarity) is not clear from the line.

161.reading: Saccandan, whose spear killed other kings and who stands among kings like a humped bull, is like a rain of honey and guards the quarters; his fame touches the sky and he has reached fullness.
161.nuance: மலிவு எய்தினான் closes the praise at a peak; the next verse begins the turn of the story with செல்வற்கு இன்னணம் சேறலில், 'while things went thus for the fortunate one'.

162.reading: While the fortunate king's life ran thus, there was the daughter of the king of well-watered Vidaiyam, a goddess even to the goddess on the lotus, with bow-long brows and eyes like thrown spears.
162.nuance: She is introduced by her father's land, not yet by name; the verse calls her an அணங்கு to the goddess Tiru herself, matching the அணங்கு the king was to women in 157. Her name, Vijayai, is given in the patikam (verse 7) and again at 182.

163.reading: Her form and grace are too rare to be matched in words, yet the poet says he will speak of the swelling beauty of the bangled girl, whom even the gods find hard to praise.
163.nuance: The poet's first person (பேசுவல்) opens a head-to-foot description (kesadi) that runs from 164 to 179.

164.reading: Her dark tresses, steeped in oil and musk, curled at the ends and full of waves, look like darkness itself wrapped in fine cloth and drawn from its sheath, and are worshipped with coloured flowers.

165.reading: Her small brow like the young crescent and her round moon of a face, her coral mouth whose pure smile grants boons to those who bow, and her nose like a flowing golden creeper would melt Urvasi herself.
165.nuance: The smile 'grants boons to those who worship it' (தொழுதற்கு வரம் கொடுக்கும்): the description borrows the language of worship for a woman's face.

166.reading: Her curved brows, shaming the beauty of the bow, slender and dark, rising over the brow and bending down to the eye's corner as if a master had painted them, are beyond all praise.

167.reading: Her eyes, like fighting carp with fine red lines at the corners and dark pupils set as if inlaid, reach to her ears and are at once poison and nectar, maddening and delighting even sages.
167.nuance: The poison-and-nectar eye echoes the king's own description in 157, poison to foes and nectar to the frightened. That the eyes move even முனிவர் (sages) to infatuation is the poem's first hint that desire can overturn the self-controlled, which the story will show in a king.

168.reading: Her long ears, shaped like scissors that cut hair, with makara earrings set in diamond that sway without rest, make the vallai leaf wither and sit in splendid colour.
168.nuance: Lines 1 and 2 (மயிர் எறி கத்தரிகை, உயிர் செகுத்து முன் ஒன்றிப் பின் பேராது) are compressed and the exact shape meant for the ear is not certain.

169.reading: Her round, beautiful neck holds in captivity the emerald of an unbearing young areca, and a rare gem that drinks darkness, like a lotus carried on darkness.
169.nuance: The comparison in lines 2 and 3 is dense; the gem that 'drinks darkness' and the lotus borne on darkness are images of the neck against her dark hair, but the syntax can be divided in more than one way.

170.reading: Her shoulders, soft as a cushion of red-lac cotton and smooth as swaying bamboo, wear pearl strings from gem makara mouths; her forearms carry bright bangles, her fingers are like red kanthal buds and her palms glow like vermilion.

171.reading: Her breasts, like a pair of caskets topped with sapphire that sends out cool rays, dark-tipped and drinking the heart, broad-based and wearing a crescent chain, are the dwelling of a goddess and spread with fair pallor spots.
171.nuance: The goddess (அணங்கு) is said to dwell in her breasts: the afflicting power of beauty is placed in the body itself.

172.reading: Her belly with a navel whirling to the right, deeper than Ganga's eddies, and a waist so slight the eye cannot hold it, such that her own people judge it exists while all others who look are left in doubt whether it is or is not.
172.nuance: The joke on the thin waist is put in the vocabulary of knowing: her own people hold by judgement (மதிப்பர்) that it exists, others are left in doubt between உண்டு and இல்லை and cannot know it. The poet plays with the terms of debate; the verse states no doctrine.

173.reading: Her broad hips, outshining a great cobra's twin hoods, a chariot's platform and a golden fan, wear a girdle that glitters and a silk red as the young sun or a small hare's blood, beyond even Indra's power to praise.

links.note: In 157 the king is fierce as a poisonous serpent's fire; in 290 he is the sun of the Kuru line swallowed by the great serpent of his minister.
links.teaches: The serpent's wrath that made Saccandan terrible to enemies is turned back on him from inside his own court, so the image of his strength becomes the image of his end.

links.note: 159 says the whole world rests in the cool shade of Saccandan's umbrella as under a father's feet; 290 says that when the minister swallows him the darkness of the bent sceptre spreads and the people grieve.
links.teaches: The shade praised as the world's settled condition proves to depend on one man's life, since one betrayal turns the straight sceptre's shade into the bent sceptre's darkness.

links.note: 167 says Vijayai's eyes are poison and nectar that madden even sages; in 181 Saccandan is caught in the net of her long eyes.
links.teaches: The descriptive claim that her eyes overturn the self-controlled is cashed in the plot: the first one they capture is the king whose fall drives the epic.

links.note: The king is an அணங்கு to women (157); the princess is an அணங்கு even to the goddess on the lotus (162).
links.teaches: The poem sets an afflicting beauty against a greater one before they meet, so the king who wounds others by his looks is the one wounded by hers.

links.note: The Kural's man sees two looks in her eyes, one that gives the sickness and one that cures it; the epic says her eyes are poison and nectar at once.
links.teaches: The couplet's private double look of lover's sickness and cure becomes, in an epic, a public force that maddens sages and later unseats a king.

gains.a: the epic's poison-and-nectar image is placed in an older Tamil account of the look as both wound and remedy
gains.b: the couplet's two looks are given consequences beyond the lover, reaching ascetics and the state

links.note: The Kural's man laments that his might, feared by enemies in battle, broke before her bright forehead; 161 shows a king whose spear killed kings at the height of his fame just before he meets Vijayai.
links.teaches: Read with the story that follows, the couplet's lover's hyperbole becomes literal history: the warrior whose strength breaks before a woman is a king, and what breaks is his kingdom.

gains.a: the praise of Saccandan's martial peak gains a known pattern that foretells its undoing by beauty
gains.b: the couplet's complaint gains a case where the broken might is public and political, not only the lover's pride

links.note: The Naladiyar says kings who rode under the umbrella at the head of armies fall when their deeds turn, and enemies take their wives; 161 shows Saccandan at the full of his fame, the starting point of such a fall.
links.teaches: The quatrain gives the general fall of the umbrella king; the epic fills in one fall step by step, with the king's own infatuation as the turn and his queen driven out, so impermanence works through character and not only fortune.

gains.a: the epic's high point of praise gains the moral frame within which its listeners would hear it as the top of a wheel
gains.b: the quatrain's abstract turn of deeds gains a narrated mechanism, desire and a trusted minister

links.note: Purananuru 35 tells the Chola his tall umbrella is not for shade but to shelter suffering subjects, and warns him the world blames kings when things go wrong; 159 says Saccandan's umbrella already shades the world like a father.
links.teaches: The Sangam poet gives the umbrella as a duty the king must be urged to keep, the epic as a state already achieved; set together, the epic's praise lacks the warning that the story will soon need.

gains.a: the epic's settled praise is seen to omit the counsel that in the Sangam poem accompanies the umbrella
gains.b: the poem's admonition gains a later narrative in which a praised umbrella king does lose the world's shade

links.note: Purananuru 56 equates the Pandya with four gods, one for each of his powers; 160 equates Saccandan with Dharma, Varuna, Death, Vaman and Kama.
links.teaches: The epic keeps the Sangam form of measuring a king god by god but shifts it from war powers to grace, giving and beauty, and puts the god of desire in the list, which the story makes the king's flaw.

gains.a: the epic's god-list is placed in an inherited praise form, so its departures (Dharma, Kama) stand out
gains.b: the Sangam form is shown surviving into Jain narrative with new gods and an ironic edge

source_issues: 154 line 1 reads பூத் கோங்கும், apparently a dropped letter (for பூத்த).
160 line 2 வாமனே is hard to construe with the comparisons around it.
